Day 1
From Hotel: 39 min · 11 min → Theatro Municipal de São Paulo
1. Theatro Municipal de São Paulo
Completed in 1911, this eclectic opera house blends French Beaux-Arts and Italian Renaissance in a gilded interior of Venetian mosaics and Carrara marble. Home to the São Paulo Symphony Orchestra, city ballet, and opera.

5 min · 2 min → Biblioteca Mário de Andrade
2. Biblioteca Mário de Andrade
Jacques Pilon's boldly geometric Art Deco landmark holds 3.2 million items, including 60000 rare manuscripts and incunabula from the 15th century. Soaring reading rooms with decorative relief set the standard for Brazilian public architecture of the era.
Read more

3 min · 2 min → Edifício Copan
3. Edifício Copan
Oscar Niemeyer's sinuous S-curve skyscraper remains the largest reinforced-concrete residential structure in Brazil. The undulating béton brut facade is the most photographed building in South America.
Read more

18 min · 5 min → Estação da Luz
4. Estação da Luz
Completed from British iron and brick shipped to São Paulo, Luz Station is the finest Victorian railway terminus in South America — a soaring clock-towered hull of cast iron, terracotta, and Art Nouveau glazing that anchors the Luz cultural quarter.

2 min · 2 min → Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo
5. Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo
Brazil's oldest state art museum, housed in Ramos de Azevedo's neoclassical brick building adjacent to Parque da Luz. The 9000-work collection — Malfatti, Rodin, Bourdelle, and Brazilian modernism — is the definitive survey of Brazilian visual art.

Day 2
From Hotel: 11 min → Catedral Metropolitana da Sé
1. Catedral Metropolitana da Sé
The neo-Gothic cathedral on Praça da Sé took over 40 years to complete and seats 8000 worshippers beneath twin 92-meter towers. The crypt below the altar holds the remains of Jesuit founder José de Anchieta, who established São Paulo in the 16th century.
Read more

~1 hr
Free
Praça da Sé · Centro
5 min · 2 min → Pátio do Colégio
2. Pátio do Colégio
On January 25, 1554, Jesuit priests José de Anchieta and Manuel da Nóbrega founded São Paulo in this hilltop clearing. The rebuilt church and Museu Anchieta hold 600 artifacts from the earliest Jesuit missions, including Anchieta's handwritten letters.
Read more

Closed Sunday & Monday
~45 min
Praça Pátio do Colégio 2 · Centro
10 min · 2 min → Liberdade
3. Liberdade
São Paulo's Japanese quarter, settled by immigrants after 1908, still hosts Brazil's largest Japanese community. Red torii-framed lampposts signal the district; the weekend street fair fills Praça da Liberdade with Japanese street food, crafts, and anime vendors.
Read more
Open 24/7

1. Mosteiro de São Bento
Benedictine monks have kept vigil on this hill since 1598. The soaring nave is encased in 17th-century carved wood, polychrome gilt altars, and icons by Frei Agostinho de Jesus — all illuminated by Gregorian chant at Sunday morning mass.

Day 4
From Hotel: 10 min → Beco do Batman
1. Beco do Batman
An unmarked alley in Vila Madalena surfaced in giant murals and tags by São Paulo's most prolific street artists, including Os Gêmeos. The walls, continuously repainted since the 1980s, form one of the world's longest-running open-air urban art galleries.

Named after Japan-born Brazilian modernist Tomie Ohtake, this Ruy Ohtake-designed arts institute programs large-scale exhibitions across 15000 sq m. The building's curved purple and orange drums are an unmistakable landmark on Avenida Faria Lima.

1. Japan House São Paulo
Opened in 2017 on Avenida Paulista, Japan House bridges contemporary Japan and Brazil through curated exhibitions, workshops, and a design shop that stocks objects unavailable outside Japan. One of three Japan Houses worldwide, it draws over a million visitors a year.

14 min → MuBE
2. MuBE
Paulo Mendes da Rocha's Pritzker Prize-winning design places sculpture below ground level in a vast open-air concrete trench, letting light and shadow become part of each installation. The permanent collection spans 5000 years of sculptural traditions across three continents.

3. Museu Lasar Segall
The former home-studio of Lithuanian-born expressionist Lasar Segall preserves 2500 works including his darkly charged São Paulo immigrant canvases, woodcuts, and Brazil series paintings — held today as a federal museum overseen by the Brazilian government.

Local Tastes
Virado à Paulista
Declared Intangible Cultural Heritage of São Paulo. Pork chop with black beans fried in manioc flour, braised kale, fried egg, rice, and banana. Served Mondays across 500000 plates citywide per week.
Bar do Juarez · Aconchego Carioca
Coxinha
Teardrop-shaped croquette of shredded chicken and cream cheese in fried dough; invented in São Paulo's factory districts.
Any padaria citywide · Mercado Municipal
Pastel de Mortadela
Thin-crust fried pastry adapted from Japanese-Brazilian spring rolls; the mortadella pastel at Mercado Municipal is the iconic street bite of São Paulo.
Mercado Municipal
Pizza Paulistana
Thin-crust wood-fired whole-pie pizza; São Paulo has more pizza restaurants per capita than any city outside Italy.
Speranza · Bráz Pizzaria
Caipirinha
Brazil's national cocktail — cachaça, sugar, and lime. Best made with artisan cachaça aged in native wood barrels from the interior of São Paulo state.
Bar Brahma · Riviera Bar

Worth Knowing

São Paulo in Layers

São Paulo's stops exist in three distinct time bands that barely overlap. The Victorian terminus at Luz was already 40 years old when the Art Deco library opened. MASP arrived while the Copan building was still new. Theatro Municipal predates all of it by more than a century. The city didn't replace one era with the next — it buried each layer and built a new city on top. Walking from Copan to the Theatro Municipal in eight minutes crosses from modernism to Beaux-Arts without transition.

The Museu Afro Brasil sits inside a Niemeyer pavilion designed for an industrial fair. Almost nothing in São Paulo is where you'd expect it to be, and that's probably the most Paulistano thing about it.
